1	# Agile Pain Relief Astro - Project Documentation
2	
3	## Project Overview
4	
5	Astro-based website for Agile Pain Relief Consulting with blog posts, glossary terms, courses, and pages.
6	
7	**Tech Stack:** Astro 7, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, MDX, TypeScript, Pagefind, Netlify
8	
9	**Build Commands:**
10	
11	- `npm run dev` - Development server with drafts enabled
12	- `npm run build` - Production build with Pagefind indexing
13	- `npm run preview` - Preview production build
14	
15	**This repo is the only source of truth for the website.** Specs, handoff docs and design briefs in Mark's Obsidian vault (or anywhere else outside the repo) are transitional working material: they get deleted, and they go stale the moment the code moves on. Never cite an external path as the authority for how something works, and never send a future reader there to find out. When such a doc informs a decision, copy the part that still matters into `CLAUDE.md`, `HISTORY.md`, an ADR, or a code comment, and drop the pointer. The exceptions are genuinely external, genuinely durable sources: vendor documentation, and the read-only material in `reference/`.
16	
17	**Change log:** `HISTORY.md` (repo root) is the plain-English "why we did it" log, newest first. After any notable change or architectural decision, add a short dated entry there. This `CLAUDE.md` documents how things work _now_; `HISTORY.md` records why they got that way. `NOTES.md` (repo root) is a terse authoring cheat-sheet (component snippets, MD-vs-MDX, gotchas) for hands-on content work.
18	
19	## Top-level directories
20	
21	- `src/` — Astro site (pages, components, content)
22	- `shared/` — Code and data used by both the Astro site and the email-automation CLI: `cakemail-constants.ts` (list/sender IDs, From name/address, form URLs), `corsizio.ts` (the Corsizio API client, used by the schedule sync and the course-email CLI but never by the site itself), and the generated `course-schedule.json`. Changes here DO trigger Netlify rebuilds.
23	- `email-automation/` — Node.js CLI for sending course emails via Cakemail. Has its own `package.json` / `tsconfig.json` / `.env`. Run commands from inside `email-automation/`. See `email-automation/CLAUDE.md` for details. Changes to this directory do NOT trigger Netlify rebuilds (see `netlify.toml`).
24	- `pandoc/` — Brand-styled Typst template and build script for turning vault markdown into lead-magnet PDFs. See "Lead-magnet PDFs" below.
25	- `docs/adr/` — Architecture Decision Records, for choices where the rejected options matter as much as the chosen one (currently: the unguessable-slug workbook gate). `CLAUDE.md` says how a thing works; an ADR says what else was considered and why it lost. Add one only when that trade-off is worth preserving.
26	- `reference/` — Read-only source material consulted while writing site content (e.g. point-in-time captures of Scrum Alliance course pages). Not code, not published, never imported by the build. See `reference/README.md`.
27	- `scripts/` — Repo-level utility scripts run through npm (`corsizio-sync.ts`, `posthog-export.ts`).
28	- `bombadil/` — Browser-test specs run by `npm run test:browser`; results land in `.bombadil-out/`.
29	- `temp/` — Scratch space for one-off previews and downloads. Not built, not shipped.
30	
31	### Post-course newsletter signup (prefilled Cakemail form)
32	
33	Post-course emails sent by `email-automation/` include a "Subscribe to the Newsletter" link pointing at `/newsletter-subscribe/` (`src/pages/newsletter-subscribe.astro`) with the student's details prefilled in the query string: `?email=…&custom_attributes[firstname]=…&auto_submit=1`. That page embeds a Cakemail form bound to the Newsletter Subscribers list (double opt-in); Cakemail's `form-prefill.js` reads the params off the page URL, fills the form, and auto-submits it. The link is built by `buildPrefillSignupUrl()` in `email-automation/src/signup-url.ts`.
34	
35	There is **no server-side endpoint, HMAC signature, or OAuth token** in this path (it predates and is separate from the Turnstile gate below). Double opt-in is the abuse guard: a forged link can only send a confirmation email to the address that owns it, which never subscribes without the click. This prefilled-link path stays fully client-side; the general newsletter form, the AI forms, and the quiz instead route through the Turnstile-gated `/api/newsletter-signup` endpoint (see "Signup bot protection" below).
36	
37	The Newsletter Subscribers list ID is not a secret and lives in `shared/cakemail-constants.ts` as `NEWSLETTER_SUBSCRIBERS_LIST_ID`.
38	
39	### Signup bot protection: Turnstile gate (`/api/newsletter-signup`)
40	
41	All browser signups except the post-course prefilled link (the general newsletter form, both AI lead-magnet forms, and the quiz capture) POST same-origin to `/api/newsletter-signup` (`src/pages/api/newsletter-signup.ts`, `prerender = false` so it deploys as a Netlify function). The function verifies a **Cloudflare Turnstile** token and only then forwards the multipart submission to one consolidated Cakemail hosted form, server-side. This replaced the old browser-direct POSTs, which exposed the raw Cakemail form URL in the client bundle where bots scraped it and submitted junk (a client-side honeypot never sees a direct POST).
42	
43	- **Turnstile keys are static (no rotation).** Public site key: a constant in `src/constants/turnstile.ts` (baked into the client bundle — a `PUBLIC_` env var would offer no advantage). Secret: Netlify env `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`, read at runtime via `process.env` so a key change needs no redeploy. **No Cakemail credentials** are involved — the hosted form accepts anonymous POSTs, so the function only verifies + forwards (this is why it's set-and-forget, unlike the old OAuth path).
44	- **The Cakemail form URL is server-only:** `src/lib/server/cakemail-forms.ts` (`CAKEMAIL_FORM_URL` + `cakemailFormUrlFor()`), removed from `shared/cakemail-constants.ts` so it never reaches the browser. One consolidated form serves every purpose; the client sends a `form` field (`newsletter` | `ai` | `quiz`) that currently all map to the one URL but leave room to split a purpose back onto its own form.
45	- **Shared widget:** `src/components/global/turnstile.tsx` (`<Turnstile onToken onExpire ref>`; loads the script once per page, explicit render). Each form keeps a `token` + `submitError`, blocks submit until a token exists, appends `cf-turnstile-response` + `form`, and resets the widget on failure. The submission is now same-origin (not `no-cors`), so the form reads the real response.

48	
49	Quizzes are authored as MDX files in `src/content/quizzes/{slug}/index.mdx` and rendered by a small, self-contained engine in `src/lib/quiz-engine/`. The engine is designed to be extractable to a standalone open-source Astro package later, so it has no imports from APR-specific code. See `src/lib/quiz-engine/README.md` for the engine's public API and authoring guide.
50	
51	Routes (APR-specific, consume the engine):
52	
53	- `/quiz/{slug}/` — landing page (`src/pages/quiz/[slug].astro`). Renders hero + category cards + persuasion block from frontmatter, then mounts the React `QuizStepper` island.
54	- `/quiz/{slug}/results/` — results page (`src/pages/quiz/[slug]/results.astro`, SSR). Dispatches on the quiz's `resultStyle` frontmatter field (`'band'` | `'map-move'`, default `'band'`). **Band** reads `?total=&max=&level=&{sectionId}={level}` and renders the matching `<ResultCard>` blocks from the quiz's MDX body. **Map-move** reads the raw answers from a single `?a=` param and renders the `MapMoveResults.astro` engine component (a per-answer map + one recommended move) directly from frontmatter, not the MDX body. If tamper-resistance becomes important, sign the query in the browser before redirect and verify on the page.

Wouldn't be easier to setup a separate list and then migrate the users over once a week?

Cleaner than what I proposed, and it solves a problem I'd written off. Worth being precise about why it works and where "once a week" breaks.

**Why it works:** tags are list-scoped. If the forms POST to a hosted form bound to a *staging* list, the replace-on-submit behaviour lands on a contact with no history to lose. The weekly job then merges them onto Newsletter Subscribers through the authenticated API, where `tagContactOnList()` **adds** rather than replaces. That dodges the blocker I'd flagged on Phase 3 — no Cakemail credential in the Netlify function, because the merge runs in `email-automation/` where the refresh token already lives and auto-rotates.

Two bonuses I didn't expect:

- It also settles the resubmit-reverts-to-`pending` risk. A repeat submitter hits the staging list, so their confirmed status on the real list is never touched.
- The staging list is a natural quarantine — junk signups are visible before they reach the main list.

**Where the weekly cadence breaks:** `aiquiz` triggers the ai-welcome series that *delivers the PDF*. Stage that, and someone waits up to seven days for the thing they just asked for. Two ways out, and I'd take the first:

- Point the ai-welcome automation at the **staging list** (triggered by list-add). Delivery is instant; the weekly job becomes pure bookkeeping and can run as slowly as you like.
- Or run the merge on a schedule rather than by hand — but then it needs a host (launchd on your machine, or a scheduled function, which reintroduces the credential problem).

**Three things it has to get right:**

- The staging form's copy must say they're subscribing to the Agile Pain Relief newsletter. The list name is internal plumbing; the form's wording is the consent. Same basis the Drip migration used for `send_double_opt_in=false`.
- The merge must skip anyone who unsubscribed or bounced on the staging list.
- Mark migrated contacts with a custom attribute so re-runs are idempotent.

Cost is roughly half a day: a list, a hosted form, a `cakemailFormUrlFor()` entry, and a `npm run migrate-signups` command (~150 lines, most of it paging contacts).

**My recommendation:** keep the Phase 1 change (forms send no tags) as the resting state — it's safe, and nothing consumes those tags today. Build the staging list when the first nurture that actually needs a tag gets built, because that's when you'll know what the merge has to carry. content.text:
Behaviour recorded in `CLAUDE.md` (and the memory file survived the revert). Now the staging design.

Your point that the staging list owns the whole sequence removes the objection I raised last time: nothing waits a week for a lead magnet, because the automation fires on the staging list at signup, and the weekly merge is pure bookkeeping.

The shape:

- Browser forms POST to a hosted form bound to a staging list. Tag replacement is harmless there because those contacts have no history on that list.
- Double opt-in happens on staging. The sequence lives there and triggers on arrival.
- `npm run migrate-signups`, weekly: page the staging list, skip unsubscribed / bounced / already-migrated, create-or-find on Newsletter Subscribers with `send_double_opt_in=false` (consent was given at the form), copy first/last name, apply tags via `tagContactOnList()` which **merges**, stamp a `migrated_at` attribute for idempotency.
- Dry-run by default, `--apply` to write.

One real fork before I build anything:

questions.question: One staging list with tags routing the sequences, or one staging list per purpose?

options.label: One list per purpose (Recommended)
options.description: Separate staging lists for newsletter / AI / quiz. Each sequence triggers on list-add, so the browser never sends a tag at all and we stop depending on tag behaviour entirely. cakemailFormUrlFor() already maps the form field to a URL, so the plumbing exists. Costs: 3 lists + 3 hosted forms to create in the UI.

options.label: One list, tags route
options.description: A single staging list; sequences trigger on aiquiz / sm-role-ai etc. One list, one form, one merge job to maintain — but the routing depends on tags landing correctly, which is the thing that just bit us.

questions.question: After a contact is merged onto Newsletter Subscribers, what happens to their staging record?

options.label: Leave them (Recommended)
options.description: Staging becomes the permanent record of how each person came in. No risk of killing a sequence that's still running. They sit on two lists; staging is never campaigned to, only automated.

options.label: Remove after the sequence ends
options.description: Keeps contact counts down and the staging list small, but needs a rule for 'sequence finished' and risks cutting someone off mid-sequence if that rule is wrong.

content.text:
One list, no tag routing. That collapses the work a long way — and it means **the site-side change is one line**, not the component churn I did last time.

The reasoning: once the hosted form is bound to staging, the replace-on-submit behaviour only ever touches staging tags, which are per-signup anyway. Newsletter Subscribers is never written to by a browser POST again. So the existing tag code can stay exactly as it is, and the merge job carries those tags across additively — attribution actually survives, which it doesn't today.

One consequence worth stating once: with a single staging list and a list-add trigger, everyone who signs up anywhere gets the same sequence, including plain newsletter and webinar signups. You've said that's fine for one lead magnet; it's a second list the day that stops being true.

39:### Signup bot protection: Turnstile gate (`/api/newsletter-signup`)
### Signup bot protection: Turnstile gate (`/api/newsletter-signup`)

All browser signups except the post-course prefilled link (the general newsletter form, both AI lead-magnet forms, and the quiz capture) POST same-origin to `/api/newsletter-signup` (`src/pages/api/newsletter-signup.ts`, `prerender = false` so it deploys as a Netlify function). The function verifies a **Cloudflare Turnstile** token and only then forwards the multipart submission to one consolidated Cakemail hosted form, server-side. This replaced the old browser-direct POSTs, which exposed the raw Cakemail form URL in the client bundle where bots scraped it and submitted junk (a client-side honeypot never sees a direct POST).

- **Turnstile keys are static (no rotation).** Public site key: a constant in `src/constants/turnstile.ts` (baked into the client bundle — a `PUBLIC_` env var would offer no advantage). Secret: Netlify env `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`, read at runtime via `process.env` so a key change needs no redeploy. **No Cakemail credentials** are involved — the hosted form accepts anonymous POSTs, so the function only verifies + forwards (this is why it's set-and-forget, unlike the old OAuth path).
- **The Cakemail form URL is server-only:** `src/lib/server/cakemail-forms.ts` (`CAKEMAIL_FORM_URL` + `cakemailFormUrlFor()`), removed from `shared/cakemail-constants.ts` so it never reaches the browser. One consolidated form serves every purpose; the client sends a `form` field (`newsletter` | `ai` | `quiz`) that currently all map to the one URL but leave room to split a purpose back onto its own form.
- **Shared widget:** `src/components/global/turnstile.tsx` (`<Turnstile onToken onExpire ref>`; loads the script once per page, explicit render). Each form keeps a `token` + `submitError`, blocks submit until a token exists, appends `cf-turnstile-response` + `form`, and resets the widget on failure. The submission is now same-origin (not `no-cors`), so the form reads the real response.

### Signup staging list (why no browser form writes to Newsletter Subscribers)

**Every browser signup lands on a staging list first.** The hosted form behind `/api/newsletter-signup` is bound to `SIGNUP_STAGING_LIST_ID`, never to Newsletter Subscribers. The reason is the tag hazard documented under "General newsletter signup" below: a hosted-form POST replaces a contact's whole tag set, and Newsletter Subscribers holds ~3,650 Drip-migrated contacts whose alumni / interest / refresher-suppression tags a single submission would wipe. A contact on the staging list has no tag history to lose, so the same POST is harmless there.

- **The welcome sequence lives on the staging list** and triggers on arrival, so a lead magnet is delivered at signup rather than waiting for the migration. That is what makes a weekly migration cadence acceptable.
- **One staging list, one sequence.** Every form (newsletter, popup, banner, webinar, AI lead magnet, quiz) feeds it, so every signup gets the same sequence. Correct while there is one lead magnet; the day that stops being true, it needs a second list rather than tag-based routing.
- **Tags are safe to send again.** Because the replace only ever hits staging, the existing `Signup*` / `From*` / `aiquiz` / quiz tags keep working, and the migration carries them onto Newsletter Subscribers *additively* — attribution now survives a second signup, which it never did before.
- **`npm run migrate-signups`** (in `email-automation/`) moves confirmed contacts across: skips anything not `active`, skips anything already stamped with a `migrated_at` custom attribute, creates on Newsletter Subscribers with `send_double_opt_in=false` (consent was given at the staging form), then applies tags via `tagContactOnList()`, which **merges**. Dry run by default; `--apply` writes; `--verbose` dumps the first raw contact; `--limit N` caps the batch. Idempotent, so re-running is free. Intended cadence is weekly, alongside the newsletter. Contacts are left on the staging list after migration and pruned by hand.
- **Second double opt-in is deliberately skipped.** The consent is the staging form's own copy, which says the person is subscribing to the Agile Pain Relief newsletter. The list name is internal plumbing. This is the same basis the Drip migration used.

## 2026-08-05 — Browser signups land on a staging list, not on Newsletter Subscribers

**Why.** We already knew a Cakemail hosted-form POST replaces a contact's whole
tag set rather than merging (verified 2026-06-02). It was written down as an
accepted trade-off, on the reasoning that "the same person signing up twice via
different widgets is rare". That reasoning only considered tags _we_ apply from a
form. The April 2026 Drip migration put 3,650 contacts on Newsletter Subscribers
carrying about four tags each — 358 with an `Alum*` tag, 554 `NewsletterAlumni`,
760 an `Interest*` tag, 2,243 a `Signup*` tag, and 21 refresher tags of which 7
are `SuppressRefresherCSM` suppressions. The first time any of them touched one
of our forms, all four would be replaced by the two or three in that submission.
Losing a suppression tag is the worst case: someone who asked not to be
contacted about refreshers, with no record left that they asked.

**Nothing was lost** — there had been no form signups in weeks.

**The first attempt was the wrong shape and was reverted.** It stripped the
`tags[...]` fields out of every form and deleted the `SignupType` / `SignupSource`
taxonomy, which meant touching seventeen files to solve the problem by giving up
the data. Mark's counter-proposal was better and much smaller: point the forms at
a **staging list** instead. Tags are list-scoped, so a contact on staging has no
history to lose and the replace behaviour becomes harmless. Newsletter Subscribers
is then only ever written to through the authenticated API, whose `/tag` endpoint
merges. The site-side change is one URL; no component changes at all, and the
signup tags keep working — in fact attribution now survives a second signup,
which it never did before.

**The staging list owns the whole automated sequence**, triggered on arrival, so
a lead magnet is delivered at signup rather than waiting on the migration. That
is what makes a weekly cadence acceptable; without it the PDF would have been up
to seven days late, which was the one serious objection to the design. One list
and one sequence is right while there is one lead magnet.

**`npm run migrate-signups`** does the crossing: skip anything not `active`, skip
anything already stamped `migrated_at`, create on Newsletter Subscribers with
`send_double_opt_in=false` (consent was given at the staging form; the list name
is plumbing), then merge the tags. Dry run by default. It reports the full status
histogram rather than only what it acted on, because the first real run is how we
learn Cakemail's status vocabulary for that list, and an unrecognised value
silently skipping people would otherwise read as "nothing to do".

**Still unverified:** whether resubmitting an already-`active` contact reverts
them to `pending` and re-sends the double opt-in. The staging list makes it much
less urgent — a resubmission now hits staging, so a confirmed newsletter
subscriber's status is never touched — but it is worth one `+alias` test.

input.old_string:
### Signup staging list (why no browser form writes to Newsletter Subscribers)

**Every browser signup lands on a staging list first.** The hosted form behind `/api/newsletter-signup` is bound to `SIGNUP_STAGING_LIST_ID`, never to Newsletter Subscribers. The reason is the tag hazard documented under "General newsletter signup" below: a hosted-form POST replaces a contact's whole tag set, and Newsletter Subscribers holds ~3,650 Drip-migrated contacts whose alumni / interest / refresher-suppression tags a single submission would wipe. A contact on the staging list has no tag history to lose, so the same POST is harmless there.

- **The welcome sequence lives on the staging list** and triggers on arrival, so a lead magnet is delivered at signup rather than waiting for the migration. That is what makes a weekly migration cadence acceptable.
- **One staging list, one sequence.** Every form (newsletter, popup, banner, webinar, AI lead magnet, quiz) feeds it, so every signup gets the same sequence. Correct while there is one lead magnet; the day that stops being true, it needs a second list rather than tag-based routing.
- **Tags are safe to send again.** Because the replace only ever hits staging, the existing `Signup*` / `From*` / `aiquiz` / quiz tags keep working, and the migration carries them onto Newsletter Subscribers *additively* — attribution now survives a second signup, which it never did before.
- **`npm run migrate-signups`** (in `email-automation/`) moves confirmed contacts across: skips anything not `active`, skips anything already stamped with a `migrated_at` custom attribute, creates on Newsletter Subscribers with `send_double_opt_in=false` (consent was given at the staging form), then applies tags via `tagContactOnList()`, which **merges**. Dry run by default; `--apply` writes; `--verbose` dumps the first raw contact; `--limit N` caps the batch. Idempotent, so re-running is free. Intended cadence is weekly, alongside the newsletter. Contacts are left on the staging list after migration and pruned by hand.
- **Second double opt-in is deliberately skipped.** The consent is the staging form's own copy, which says the person is subscribing to the Agile Pain Relief newsletter. The list name is internal plumbing. This is the same basis the Drip migration used.
input.new_string:
### Two signup destinations: main list, or staging list

A signup goes to one of two Cakemail hosted forms, decided **server-side** by `cakemailFormFor()` in `src/lib/server/cakemail-forms.ts` from the `form` field the client sends. The split exists because of the tag hazard documented under "General newsletter signup" below: a hosted-form POST replaces a contact's whole tag set, and Newsletter Subscribers holds ~3,650 Drip-migrated contacts whose alumni / interest / refresher-suppression tags one submission would wipe.

| `form` value | Destination | Tags | Follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `newsletter` | Newsletter Subscribers, directly | **stripped** | the single welcome email, triggered on list-add |
| `ai`, `quiz` | Signup Staging list | forwarded | the lead-magnet sequence, triggered on arrival there |

- **Stripping is what makes the direct path safe.** A POST with no `tags[<name>]=true` field leaves the contact's existing tags untouched. The endpoint drops those fields when `tagPolicy` is `strip`, in `src/pages/api/newsletter-signup.ts` — enforced there rather than in each form component, because that is the one place that knows the destination and a future component author cannot forget it. The `Signup*` / `From*` tags those forms still send are simply discarded; nothing consumes them.
- **The inline `<Newsletter>` form is the `newsletter` path**, and it appears on ~16 pages under a dozen different promises ("get your free copy", "join the Effective Scrum waitlist", "get your free invitation"). All of them are answered by the one welcome email (`email-automation/automations/welcome-newsletter/`), which carries the ebook and lean-coffee links. That is why they don't need staging: no sequence to route, no tag to preserve.
- **Staging carries only the paths that need a sequence and use tags** — the quiz and the two AI lead-magnet forms. A contact there has no tag history to lose, so the replace behaviour is harmless, and the sequence triggers on arrival so the lead magnet is delivered at signup rather than waiting for the migration.
- **`npm run migrate-signups`** (in `email-automation/`) moves confirmed staging contacts onto Newsletter Subscribers: skips anything not `active`, skips anything already stamped with a `migrated_at` custom attribute, creates with `send_double_opt_in=false` (consent was given at the staging form), then applies tags via `tagContactOnList()`, which **merges**. Dry run by default; `--apply` writes; `--verbose` dumps the first raw contact; `--limit N` caps the batch. Idempotent. Intended cadence is weekly, alongside the newsletter. Contacts stay on staging afterwards and are pruned by hand.
- **Second double opt-in is deliberately skipped** on migration. The consent is the staging form's own copy, which says the person is subscribing to the Agile Pain Relief newsletter; the list name is internal plumbing. Same basis the Drip migration used.
- **Unset staging URL fails soft, not closed.** If `CAKEMAIL_STAGING_FORM_URL` is empty, an `ai`/`quiz` signup still goes through — to the main list, untagged, with a loud `console.error`. Losing the person is worse than losing their sequence, and nothing gets destroyed.
- **The post-course prefilled link (`/newsletter-subscribe/`) is a third path** that bypasses this endpoint entirely: it embeds a Cakemail form bound to Newsletter Subscribers and sends no tags, so it is safe as-is and gets the welcome email like any other main-list signup.

No new automation needed — the welcome email you described already exists. `astro check` is clean (0/0/0), Tailwind lint clean, `tsc` clean on the CLI.

**Where it landed:**

| Path | Destination | Tags | Follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Inline `<Newsletter>` (~16 pages) | Newsletter Subscribers, direct | stripped | existing welcome email |
| Post-course prefilled link | Newsletter Subscribers, direct | none already | existing welcome email |
| Quiz, AI lead magnet ×2 | Signup Staging | forwarded | new sequence, on arrival |

The strip is enforced in `/api/newsletter-signup`, not in the components — that endpoint already chooses the destination, so destination and tag policy are decided in one place and a future form author can't forget it. `cakemailFormFor()` returns `{ url, tagPolicy }`. **No component was touched**, so the signup forms are byte-identical to what's in production.

**Still yours to do:**

1. `npm run refresh-cakemail` — token is fully expired, nothing else runs until it's minted.
2. `npm run create-list -- "Signup Staging"` → paste the id into `SIGNUP_STAGING_LIST_ID`.
3. Create the staging hosted form in the UI → give me the URL for `CAKEMAIL_STAGING_FORM_URL`. Until then the quiz and AI forms keep working, going to the main list untagged with a loud log.
4. Build the lead-magnet sequence on staging, triggered on list-add.
5. `npm run migrate-signups -- --verbose` and send me the output — it dumps the first contact verbatim so I can confirm the `tags` / `status` field shapes I had to guess without a token.

content.text:
**Answer: no GUI for the list.** What's scriptable and what isn't:

| Step | How |
| --- | --- |
| Create the list | `npm run create-list -- "Signup Staging"` — API |
| Register its custom attributes | `npm run ensure-newsletter-attributes` — API |
| Create the hosted form on it | **GUI** |
| Build the sequence | **GUI** |

The attributes step was missing from the sequence I gave you earlier, and it's not optional: Cakemail attributes are list-scoped and must exist before anything can set them. Without it the form's `custom_attributes[firstname]` would be rejected on first submission, and `migrate-signups` couldn't write its `migrated_at` marker — so the idempotency guard would silently never engage and every run would re-migrate everyone. I've extended that command to cover both lists; it skips staging with instructions while the id is empty.

I can't tell you whether Cakemail's API can create the *form* — I'd need a working token to check, and the repo has no precedent for it. `email-automation/CLAUDE.md` listed forms as a manual UI step, which is the only evidence either way, so plan on the GUI.

1. `npm run refresh-cakemail`
2. `npm run create-list -- "Signup Staging"` → paste the id into `SIGNUP_STAGING_LIST_ID`
3. `npm run ensure-newsletter-attributes` → confirms both lists
4. GUI: hosted form on the staging list (double opt-in) → send me the URL
5. GUI: the sequence, triggered on list-add
6. `npm run migrate-signups -- --verbose`

Two Cakemail facts worth having, now in `email-automation/CLAUDE.md`:

- **There are two form object types.** `POST /forms` (page-builder, `form_submission/<hash>`) returns a 500 on create even with a minimal payload — the client retried four times, so it's not transient. `POST /lists/{id}/forms` works and makes a `subscription_form_endpoint` (`subscription_forms/<hash>`): a bare POST target, no page builder. The submission failed, and I think I've found why — but the fix is yours to make, not mine.

**Result:** `500 fatal_error`, no contact created, no DOI email sent. Nothing to clean up.

**Cause:** the only functional difference between the two lists is one field:

| | Newsletter Subscribers | Signup Staging |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `policy_accepted` | `true` | **`false`** |
| `default_sender` | contact@ | mark@ |

`policy_accepted` is Cakemail's anti-spam attestation — the confirmation that contacts added to the list have genuinely opted in. A list created through the API starts unaccepted, which fits: the working list was made in the UI, where you'd have ticked it. A list that hasn't been accepted refusing all subscriptions is exactly the behaviour you'd expect, and it's the only candidate the data offers.

I'm not going to set that one for you. It's a compliance affirmation in your name, not a config value, and clicking it on your behalf is not mine to do.

Two ways to clear it:

- Tick it in the Cakemail UI under the Signup Staging list's settings, or
- Tell me to send `PATCH /lists/9452554 {"policy_accepted": true}` and I'll run it.

Worth checking while you're there whether `default_sender` should be `contact@` to match the other list — I set it from `SENDER_ID_MARK` because that's what `create-list.ts` hardcodes, but the working newsletter list uses `contact@`.

Once it's accepted, `npx tsx src/_probe-staging-submit.ts` re-runs the test (takes an optional `+alias` argument). It POSTs the exact payload the endpoint forwards and reads the contact back, so one run tells us whether `custom_attributes[firstname]` and `tags[...]` both land — which is the assumption the whole staging design rests on.

`policy_accepted` is silently ignored on both PATCH and POST — the API accepts the request, returns 200/201, and leaves it `false`. It's UI-only, which for a spam-policy affirmation is arguably correct behaviour on Cakemail's part.

content.text:
`policy_accepted` can't be set through the API at all — ignored on both `POST /lists` and `PATCH /lists/{id}`, and both still return 2xx. Confirmed on a throwaway list, which I've deleted.

So the list has to be made in the UI, where that policy is presented. I've documented the trap in `email-automation/CLAUDE.md` and made `create-list` print a warning, because "created a list, forms silently do nothing, no error anywhere" is a nasty half-hour to lose twice.

One caveat on the diagnosis: I can only see that the UI-created list works and the API-created one doesn't, and `policy_accepted` is the only visible difference. There could be another invisible difference between UI-created and API-created lists. It doesn't change what to do — the remedy is the same either way.

**What's needed from you:**

content.text:
No — and it would break the signups.

The browser never touches the Cakemail form: our own form is Turnstile-gated, and the Netlify function forwards server-side. reCAPTCHA would demand a `g-recaptcha-response` token that a server-to-server POST can't mint, so every signup would fail. The live Newsletter Signup form has it disabled too (`recaptcha: {secret: null, domain: null, site_key: null}`), which is the working reference.

The one thing it would theoretically cover is the form's `published_url` hosted page, which is publicly submittable and bypasses Turnstile. It's not linked anywhere, and if bots ever find it the fix is to rotate the form, not to add a challenge our server can't answer.

39	 * fault, not the list.

44	 */
45	export const CAKEMAIL_STAGING_FORM_URL =

50	 * `strip` is not a nicety: a tagged POST to a Newsletter Subscribers form
51	 * silently destroys that contact's existing tags.
52	 */

54	
55	/**
56	 * Resolve where a signup goes and whether its tags may travel with it.
57	 *
58	 * - `newsletter` — straight onto Newsletter Subscribers, tags STRIPPED. These
59	 *   forms make a plain subscribe promise ("get your free copy", "join the
60	 *   waitlist") and are answered by the single welcome email that triggers on
61	 *   list-add. Their `Signup*` / `From*` tags have no consumer, and forwarding
62	 *   them would wipe whatever the contact already carries.
63	 * - `ai` / `quiz` — onto the staging list, tags forwarded. Harmless there, and
64	 *   the sequence and the migration both read them.
65	 *
66	 * Unknown or missing values fall through to the safe destination.
67	 */
68	export function cakemailFormFor(target: string | null): {
69	  url: string;
70	  tagPolicy: TagPolicy;
71	} {
72	  if (target === 'ai' || target === 'quiz') {
73	    // Fail SOFT, not closed: without a staging form we still take the signup —
74	    // on the main list, with tags stripped, so nothing is destroyed. Losing the
75	    // person would be worse than losing their sequence, but this is a
76	    // misconfiguration and needs to be shouted about.
77	    if (!CAKEMAIL_STAGING_FORM_URL) {
78	      console.error(
79	        `CAKEMAIL_STAGING_FORM_URL is unset; routing "${target}" signup to the main list untagged. ` +
80	          'The lead-magnet sequence will NOT fire for this contact.'
81	      );
82	      return { url: CAKEMAIL_FORM_URL, tagPolicy: 'strip' };
83	    }
84	    return { url: CAKEMAIL_STAGING_FORM_URL, tagPolicy: 'forward' };
85	  }

tasks.task_name: Report to Cakemail: API-created lists silently discard every form signup
tasks.note:
Found 2026-08-05 while building the signup staging list. Cost about an hour to diagnose because nothing anywhere reports an error.

PRIMARY BUG — the API lets you create a list, then doesn't honour it.

A list created with POST /lists gets policy_accepted: false. Any signup form bound to that list then DISCARDS every submission while reporting success: the form returns its normal 302 to the double-opt-in page, and no contact is created, no confirmation email is sent, and nothing is logged. From the caller's side it is indistinguishable from a working signup. The account had already accepted the permission policy, so this is not a first-time-setup prompt.

Worse, there is no API route to correct it:
- POST /lists with policy_accepted: true  -> 201, field ignored, stays false
- PATCH /lists/{id} with policy_accepted: true -> 422 "At least one parameter must be provided" (field not in schema)
- PATCH /lists/{id} with {name, policy_accepted: true} -> 200, name applied, flag still false

The only fix is to delete the list and recreate it in the UI, which sets the flag silently (no policy is shown, presumably because the account accepted it previously).

Reproduction:
1. POST /lists {name, default_sender, language} -> note the id
2. GET /lists/{id} -> policy_accepted: false
3. Create a signup form on that list in the UI
4. POST email + custom_attributes[firstname] to the form's submission_url
5. 302 to the double-opt-in page as normal; GET /lists/{id}/contacts is empty; no email arrives
6. Same POST to a form on a UI-created list creates a pending contact within seconds

Ask: either honour policy_accepted on POST /lists, or make it settable via PATCH, or — at minimum — have submissions to an unaccepted list return an error instead of a success redirect. The silent success is the real defect; the missing setter is just inconvenient.

SECONDARY, worth a sentence in the same ticket (both surface loudly, both have a UI workaround):
- POST /forms returns 500 "Internal communication error" on create, even with a minimal {name, list_id}. Retried four times.
- POST /lists/{id}/forms succeeds and returns a subscription_form_endpoint with a subscription_forms/<hash> submission URL, but every POST to that URL returns 500. Confirmed against the known-good Newsletter Subscribers list too, so it is the endpoint type rather than the list.

Full write-up with the evidence is in HISTORY.md (2026-08-05, staging list entry) and the gotchas section of email-automation/CLAUDE.md. Claude has the exact request/response pairs and offered to draft the ticket text.
